tagline: Country roads connect colonial churches, river ports and Maryland’s first capital
intro: Tree-lined backroads cross rolling farmland on Southern Maryland’s Religious Freedom Byway, passing red-brick colonial homes and views of the Potomac. The Federal Highway Administration identifies it as a National Scenic Byway whose branches reach toward the river, linking early churches with Maryland’s colonial capital. Maryland’s tourism office allows five to seven hours for the drive from Port Tobacco to Point Lookout.

The places joined by this route grew from a colony intended as a haven for Catholic and Protestant Christians. That promise coexisted with slavery. At Port Tobacco, traders imported enslaved Africans for sale and bondage in the surrounding community. Christ Church Durham Parish traces its charter to 1692; the present brick building dates from the 1730s. The byway also passes living congregations: Piscataway families belong to St. Ignatius parish today.

Start with the Port Tobacco loop, traveling west to Christ Church Durham Parish and onward to Smallwood State Park before returning to Port Tobacco. Continue toward Chapel Point, then east to Chaptico. A branch south to Coltons Point leads to the museum serving St. Clement’s Island. The onward journey reaches Leonardtown, Piney Point and Historic St. Mary’s City before finishing at Point Lookout, where a Civil War prison camp occupied the peninsula.

moments.title: Port Tobacco
moments.text: In the 1760s, the port shipped a million pounds of tobacco each year. Port Tobacco lost its water connection before it lost its place as county seat. Erosion from farming and poor soil conservation filled the river with silt, blocking larger merchant vessels and reducing port commerce by the Civil War. A Baltimore and Potomac Railroad line bypassed the town in 1873; La Plata became county seat in 1895. The courthouse now houses a museum with exhibits on tobacco and archaeological finds from early colonial and Native American life. It is also a National Underground Railroad Network to Freedom site.

moments.title: St. Clement's Island
moments.text: St. Clement’s Island served as a temporary base for Maryland’s arriving colonists in 1634 while they negotiated with the Yaocomico for land for a permanent settlement. Jesuit Father Andrew White celebrated the first Roman Catholic Mass in the British-American colonies here. The island’s stone cross was erected in 1934 to mark Maryland’s three hundredth anniversary. The lighthouse belongs to a later act of commemoration: the St. Clement’s Hundred community organization completed the replica in 2008. Its predecessor stood from 1851 until fire destroyed it in 1956. The island lies in the Potomac River, half a mile southeast of Coltons Point.
moments.notice: The lighthouse is a replica completed in 2008; the stone cross dates to 1934.

moments.title: Historic St. Mary's City
moments.text: The State House at Historic St. Mary’s City is a reconstruction. The original brick building was completed in 1676 and dismantled in 1829. Its site lies beneath the neighboring Trinity Episcopal churchyard. When the capital moved to Annapolis, the former town center became farmland, leaving archaeological remains below ground. The living-history museum and archaeology site now interprets that settlement through exhibits including the reconstructed State House, a tobacco plantation and a replica Maryland Dove. The original Dove was one of two ships that brought Maryland’s first settlers. Archaeological research continues here alongside the reconstructed colonial buildings.

practical: St. Clement's Island: Island access is by private boat or seasonal water taxi from the St. Clement’s Island Museum at Coltons Point. (checked 2026-10-11)
